facts.text: Speedo launched the LZR Racer swimsuit in February 2008; NASA’s Langley Research Center helped test its fabrics and seams for drag.
At the 2008 Beijing Olympics, swimmers wearing the LZR Racer won 94 percent of the swimming gold medals and set 23 of the 25 world records broken there.
The LZR Racer included polyurethane panels; later suits made entirely of polyurethane, such as the Arena X-Glide and suits by Jaked, were faster still.
Polyurethane suits are impermeable: they keep water out and can trap air between the suit and the body, so swimmers float higher and meet less drag.
At the 2009 world swimming championships in Rome, held over about one week, 43 world records were broken.

In Rome in 2009, Michael Phelps, wearing a Speedo LZR Racer, lost the 200m freestyle to Paul Biedermann, who wore an all-polyurethane Arena X-Glide; it was Phelps’s first major individual defeat in four years.
Many swimmers had sponsorship deals that kept them from switching to a rival company’s faster suit.
Swimming’s governing body had approved the suits; in 2009 it reversed an earlier decision to ban the all-polyurethane models, so they could be worn in Rome.
From 2010, swimming’s governing body banned polyurethane and other non-textile suits; men’s suits may run only from the waist to the knee, and women’s from the shoulder to the knee.
In 2009 critics warned that the suit-era records might stay unbeaten for generations once the suits were banned.
After the ban, the suit-era world records began to fall again within a short time, broken by swimmers in suits that met the new rules.
The power needed to overcome drag rises with the cube of speed, so a swimmer must spend about 33 percent more energy to become 10 percent faster.
Before the polyurethane suits, the last change in racing-suit technology of similar importance was the switch from nylon to Lycra in the early 1970s.
A sports researcher argues that elite performance always combines natural ability with training and technology, and rules on equipment across sports often draw somewhat arbitrary lines.
Critics called the suits a form of technological doping.
